title: BashMCP: Give agents a terminal for your website
pitch: Add one line of code to expose WebMCP actions as composable shell commands. Agents can inspect, filter, and chain them, saving hundreds of tool calls and up to 83% of token usage.
about_excerpt: Add one line of code to expose WebMCP actions as composable shell commands. Agents can inspect, filter, and chain them, saving hundreds of tool calls and up to 83% of token usage. Like Comment Story Updates 10/10 correct versus 2/10 natively, with 59–75% fewer tokens and 99–100% fewer calls and bytes. The same real agent and task: both carts correct, with 17 calls natively versus 3 with BashMCP. Live-store turn collapse: 517 host-visible calls become 2; 1.15 MB returned becomes 4.4 KB. One WebMCP tool named bash compiles site tools into /bin; tool save registers a new WebMCP tool. A saved pipeline becomes a WebMCP tool that the next agent finds and runs without being told. A browser-native computer: site and network files, typed commands with help, and persistent SQLite. BashMCP runs on any website, with or without existing tools; Shopify is the worked example. BashMCP: a command line inside any website. One script tag adds a site-side runtime above the WebMCP standard. WebMCP makes a website callable. BashMCP makes it a computer, and the computer gets better every visit. <script src="https://bashmcp.apptory.ai/bashmcp.js" data-bashmcp data-ui="drawer"></script> That is the whole install. BashMCP is a site-side WebMCP composition runtime that installs into an existing website and runs inside that page's live session—not a separate browser VM, a hosted sandbox, or a replacement for the site's tools. One tag boots a sandboxed Unix-like workspace inside the page's own origin. Every WebMCP tool the site already registers compiles into a typed shell command. The page's own network traffic becomes files. An origin-scoped SQLite database persists across tabs and visits. The primary composition entry point registers back into WebMCP as a tool named bash , whose input is { command } —the same string a person would type at a terminal. A separate read-only dom page reader is registered beside it. On the demo store, an agent composes Shopify's ten existing WebMCP tools with jq , grep , sort , and SQL in one auditable run instead of returning every intermediate result to model context. Measured with a blind GPT-5.6 Sol agent on a whole-catalog size audit, that turned 2 of 10 correct into 9 of 10 , while reducing a native median of 315 model-visible host calls to 2 . The person watching sees the same pipeline land in a shared terminal, can rerun or edit it, and can save it as a new WebMCP tool. Fresh agents found and reused such a saved tool unprompted in 14 of 15 measured warm sessions. Same-origin only. No host shell. Shopify is the worked example, not the boundary. The numbers first Same agent, same task, same store, and the same Shopify tools available in both conditions. The prompts never mention bash or prescribe a method. The design and primary metrics were declared before the first benchmark cell ran, exact verifiers read the resulting cart, and every failure is published. Task Site tools alone Same tools, bash beside them What it shows Whole-catalog size audit, clone, n=10 2/10 correct; median 315 calls 9/10 correct; 2 calls Local composition can finish work that serial model-visible calls often cannot Whole-catalog category census, clone, n=10 2/10 correct 10/10 correct The agent chose the shell unprompted in every whole-catalog run Three-step shopper session with a real cart mutation, live store, n=8 3/8 correct 8/8 correct; 41% fewer tokens [23–65%] Query, ranking, and mutation on the production store Single product lookup, control, n=10 10/10 correct 10/10 correct; 2% more tokens ; bash unused in 7/10 The shell adds no value where there is nothing to compose Saved tool reused by a fresh agent, n=15 — 14/15 found it; 15/15 correct; 67% fewer tokens The site's tool surface compounds 500-product catalog audit, n=4 0/4 completed; up to 1,545 calls 3/4 completed in 2–4 calls The benefit increases as the fan-out grows A host-visible call is a call the host makes on the model's behalf whose result enters model context. The site tools invoked inside a bash program still execute against the real application, and every nested call remains visible in the run receipt. BashMCP removes repeated model round trips; it does not hide or eliminate the underlying application work. We make no comparative wall-clock or cost claim. The shell is often slower on a single action, which is why the flat control remains in every results table. The complete methodology, intervals, provenance, and failure ledger are in docs/results.md . Why BashMCP is a strong fit for WebMCP In agent hosts today, broad tasks often become serial tool executions: each result returns to model context before the model decides what to call next. That is exactly right for one action— add this item to my cart or show me that variant . It becomes expensive and brittle when work spans an entire dataset. Auditing every product, ranking a catalog, or cross-referencing endpoints can require hundreds of model-visible round trips, each adding another payload the model must consume before continuing. The tools were not the problem. The turns were. The site's tools remain the correct, authoritative actions. BashMCP never reimplements them. It changes where their composition happens: search, filtering, ranking, joining, and mutation execute as one local program, while only the final answer returns to model context. A host could add batching or a code interpreter for its own users. A site-installed environment has three different advantages: It runs inside the visitor's live session. It can work with the current cart, prices, stock, locale, login state, and the person's own actions without exporting that state into a separate environment. Persistence belongs to the origin. Saved tools, history, and the database remain in the site's browser origin and are available on later visits. The tool surface ships with the site. Anything the site registers can help compatible agents from multiple hosts, and a developer can promote an agent-authored tool into the site's build for future visitors. So we asked: What is the most useful thing a site can register through WebMCP? Our answer was an environment rather than another verb. A better experience for the agent and the person For the agent , BashMCP provides a POSIX-shaped environment it already understands: a filesystem to explore, commands with familiar flags, pipes, exit codes, man pages, --help , jq , grep , sort , and SQL. It does not require a long instruction manual in the tool description. The description points the agent toward cat /README.md , tools , man <command> , and --help ; the environment teaches the rest. In every measured whole-catalog run, the agent selected bash without being told to use it while Shopify's ten original tools remained available. For the person , the developer installation mounts a shared terminal beside the page: One transcript. Two identities: you@host and agent@host . One command history. One filesystem. live_observation.first_impression: Aubrene is a Shopify-style clothing store with products, cart/search/account controls, and an open-looking BashMCP console area.
live_observation.action_attempted: Clicked the CHOOSE button for a featured trouser product.
live_observation.after_state: The store remained on the collection view in the accessible state; no confirmed cart or product-detail transition was observable.
live_observation.notes: The console is represented by Terminal/Runs/Tools/Events tabs and a textbox, but no agent credentials or commands were entered.
